When my father retired, he started putting the wrong things in the little free library at the end of our street. First a tin of buttons, then two good hinges in a sandwich bag. My mother made him go back for the hinges.

“It says library, Martin.”

“Somebody might be looking for hinges.”

“Not there.”

He went back after supper. The hinges were gone.

For several days he bore this vindication quietly. Then a note appeared inside the library, folded around a short pencil: *If the person who left the hinges has any more, I could use one for the other side.*

My father had twenty or thirty hinges in the garage. He took them all down to the library in a biscuit tin and waited on the bench across the street. At lunchtime my mother brought him a cheese sandwich. At three she brought him his hat. At five a girl of about twelve came by on a bicycle, opened the tin, and began comparing hinges against something she had drawn on her wrist.

“Center to center,” my father called.

She looked around.

“The screw holes. It’s easier to measure from one center to the other.”

“I traced it,” she said, holding up her arm. There, in blue ink, was the outline of a hinge, complete with three solemn dots.

“Even better,” he admitted.

She was building a cupboard for her little brother, who had begun collecting stones and needed somewhere to put them. Their mother had said that if she found one more stone in the washing machine she was moving to a hotel.

“How many stones?” my father asked.

The girl considered. “Do you mean good ones?”

He came home delighted. Here was a person, he said, who understood the importance of asking what was actually being counted.

I visited that weekend. On Saturday morning he took me to see the cupboard. The girl had installed it against the fence in her backyard, low enough for her brother to reach. It was painted a violent orange. The door hung a little crooked, and on the front, in green marker, someone had written MUSEAM.

My father and I stood outside the gate while the boy, who was perhaps five, showed us the collection. There was a white stone with a hole in it. There was a piece of brick. There was a lump of asphalt with a yellow stripe, which had once been part of a road and was therefore, he explained, the only stone in the museum that knew where anything was.

“And this one?” I asked. It was a plain gray pebble in the middle of the shelf.

“That one’s just holding my place.”

“For what?”

He shrugged. Apparently I had asked the sort of question adults ask when they have never run a museum.

On the walk home, my father stopped twice to examine the ground. The second time he picked up a small green marble, clouded and chipped.

“Do you think he’d want this?”

“You can ask him.”

“No,” he said after a moment. “I think I want it.”

He put it in his pocket.

For the rest of his life, which was another eleven years, that marble sat in the shallow wooden dish beside his bed, among the practical things he took off or put on each day: watch, glasses, wedding ring when his knuckles swelled. After he died, my mother tipped the contents of the dish into my hands so she could dust under it. I recognized the marble by touch before I looked down.

“I wondered where that came from,” she said.

I told her about the orange cupboard and the piece of road. I told her about the girl with the hinge drawn on her wrist. My mother sat down on the edge of the bed, still holding the dust cloth.

“He never told me that part.”

I nearly said, *I thought he told you everything.* Instead I asked which part.

“The wrist,” she said. “I’d have liked that.”

She took the marble out of my palm and held it up to the window. In the light it was not quite green. There was blue in it, and a twist of white glass so fine you could lose it by turning the marble a fraction.

“Look at that,” she said, and handed it back.

We went on passing it between us for a while, each finding something the other had missed.
